1. Outside view. The base rate for the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment index is highly anchored to its preliminary release. Historically, the final reading deviates from the mid-month preliminary reading by an average absolute margin of about 1.0 to 1.5 index points, as both are derived from overlapping survey samples. A naive extrapolation predicts the final reading will be exactly the preliminary reading of 51.0.

2. Inside view. The preliminary August 2026 reading was reported at 51.0 on August 14, dropping significantly from July's 55.2 due to inflation fears tied to a Middle East conflict and a drop in retail sales. Between the mid-month cutoff and the end of the month, respondents completing the survey will continue to absorb the negative retail sales data and the ongoing geopolitical news. While late-month sentiment could drift slightly lower as negative headlines percolate, these factors are mostly priced into the initial 51.0 print. There are no major data releases scheduled in the intervening two weeks that would confidently drive the index more than a point in either direction. I will adjust the expected value a hair downward to 50.9 to reflect the lingering pessimism.

3. Pre-mortem. If this forecast is badly wrong, it will be because late-August respondents reacted strongly to an acute, unpriced event—such as a sudden spike in gasoline prices stemming from the mentioned Middle East/Iran conflict, or a sharp stock market selloff. If this occurred, the final reading could be revised downward by up to 3 points. To correct for this fat-tail geopolitical risk, I should widen my standard deviation slightly beyond the normal peacetime revision range.

4. Calibrate. Normally, the standard deviation of the revision from preliminary to final is about 1.2 points. To encompass the potential for a larger-than-usual mid-month shift due to the volatile inflation and geopolitical backdrop, a standard deviation of 1.3 is appropriately cautious, ensuring the true value lands within one standard deviation about 68% of the time.

{"mean": 50.9, "sd": 1.3}
